A worked example from an evaluation, not a recommendation. It shows one end of the turnkey↔build spectrum as it was actually built and measured. The two ends side by side, and when to pick which: Which RAG engine?

Running RAGFlow

RAG built as a turnkey appliance — RAGFlow. It runs headless behind a chatbot: it hands back ranked chunks, our app writes the answer. This is a worked example of the turnkey end of the RAG spectrum — the opposite end being a build assembled from scratch on a framework like Spring AI, against the same retrieval contract. Every artifact below is captured from the live stack, not drawn.

concept → implementation1Introducing RAGFlow

This page is the build: given the standard RAG pipeline — parse → chunk → embed → index → retrieve — how do we actually assemble one? You could hand-assemble every box yourself, or take an engine that ships them assembled. We took the engine. It's called RAGFlow, and it runs as a headless retrieval service behind a chatbot.

Why RAGFlow: it's a turnkey appliance for exactly that pipeline. DeepDoc parsing (OCR + table structure, §2), hybrid dense+sparse retrieval, and RAPTOR + GraphRAG — all out of the box, all drivable through a documented /api/v1. We run it headless (no RAGFlow UI, no RAGFlow answer-LLM): it returns ranked chunks and our app writes the answer, so the calling agent stays in control of how the evidence is combined.

What RAGFlow is made of

Not one process — a small multi-datastore appliance. One API server fronts four backing stores; a retrieval call fans out to them and back (each store named with the env var that selects it):

API server Flask · /api/v1 · the only surface we touch
Postgresmetadata
DB_TYPE=postgres
Infinityvectors · chunks · search
DOC_ENGINE=infinity
OpenDAL-fsoriginal file bytes
STORAGE_IMPL=OPENDAL
Redistask queue + cache
(Valkey here)

This is the hardened stack we run (§2 bridges to the living corpus) — Infinity for vectors and search and OpenDAL-fs for blobs, not the default Elasticsearch + MinIO. Leaner footprint, same /api/v1. Redis isn't optional — it's the job broker (Redis Streams) every parse/index task flows through, plus cache. We run Valkey, a drop-in.

Each backing role is swappable — pick your backend

RAGFlow fixes the four roles, not the products behind them. Three of the four are a single env var pointing at a different backend; only the task broker isn't a menu. (This is what "fixed backing stores" really means — the shape is fixed, the implementations are yours to choose.)

Where RAGFlow sits in the field

It's a crowded field — a Spring AI hand-build, NVIDIA's RAG Blueprint, Dify, the incremental-native graph engines (LightRAG · fast-GraphRAG · LazyGraphRAG), and more. Each occupies a different point on the build-it-yourself ↔ buy-it-assembled spectrum, and weighing them fairly is its own exercise; this page isn't that verdict. RAGFlow is simply a worked example of the turnkey end — an appliance that ships the whole pipeline assembled.

reversible RAGFlow isn't welded in. It sits behind one seam — our reconciler on the write side and a single read-side retrieval client on the other (the §4 seam). Swapping the engine is an adapter-backend change, not a pipeline rewrite. So this is a current implementation choice, not an irreversible decision.

How much of RAGFlow can you actually change?

A turnkey appliance, but not a black box you can't reach into. RAGFlow is a fixed, opinionated pipeline with four degrees of control on top. A piece's model and its step are independent axes, so some wear two badges.

our actual ingestion2Ingestion, for real — DeepDoc reads what plain text can't

Now the concrete version of ingestion — parse → chunk → embed → index — on our stack. Step 1 (parse) is the one that earned RAGFlow its footprint. RAGFlow ships its own parser, DeepDoc (OCR + table-structure + layout) — and on a scanned, image-only PDF, plain text extraction recovers nothing while DeepDoc recovers a structured table.

See it for yourself. On the left is the literal file — a photo of a page, no selectable text. On the right is what the dumb tool gets. Below is the real, full DeepDoc output that actually went into the index (scroll it — it's authentic, glitches and all).

the file · gear-care-scanned.pdf (both pages)

honest caveat DeepDoc works out of the box because it's not an LLM — it's RAGFlow's built-in OCR + table models running on plain CPU, no GPU and no API key. The flip side: it's OCR, so it slips digits and words (than→thap, 一 for a dash) and packs ~3 physical rows into each <tr> (the multi-value cells above). Good enough to retrieve and ground on; not a clean raw-extract. And it's a config knob, not a rewrite — RAGFlow ships the parser as a per-dataset menu (DeepDoc · MinerU · Docling · Naive · OpenDataLoader); we kept the DeepDoc default because it's the zero-GPU, zero-key one. For real fidelity we'd flip to Docling (model-swappable) or upgrade the parse stage to an accelerated LLM/VLM parser (Nemotron-Parse), captured as a deferred plan.

RAPTOR & GraphRAG are separate dataset-level index tasks (POST /datasets/{id}/index?type=raptor|graph), built by an unguarded local-chat lane at ingest — the base parse trigger never dispatches them. Global and compute-heavy: both fire many LLM calls, and adding one doc reclusters the whole tree — a full rebuild every time, not an incremental top-up. The expense is compute, not wall-clock: on production GPUs it's fast but never free, and the cost scales with corpus × edit-frequency. More on what that means for a living corpus next.

living corpus "Built once" is only half true. The corpus is watched and reconciled: when a source document is added, edited, or deleted, the vector layer reparses just that doc and the index stays in sync — incremental, near-instant (~seconds for one doc). The catch is the deep layer: RAPTOR & GraphRAG are a global recompute — one new doc reclusters the whole tree via many LLM calls. It's not really wall-clock (on real GPUs it's quick) — it's that the compute cost scales with corpus × edit-frequency, so re-running it on every edit is wasteful. Hence: off by default, lit on a schedule — a periodic batch job for a relatively static corpus, not per-edit. The vector layer carries the live churn; the deep layer is a scheduled regenerate. The net effect: adds, edits and deletes to a source document flow into retrieval within seconds via the vector layer, while the RAPTOR/GraphRAG trees catch up on their scheduled batch.

our actual retrieval3Retrieval, for real — and how the agent drives it

First: who's asking? The agentic loop calls RAG in parallel

A real upstream agent (we haven't built the loop yet — picture it) doesn't fire one vague query. It decomposes a fuzzy ask into several sharp, independent questions and fires them at RAG in parallel, then reasons over the merged chunks.

agent
"Can I return my worn-out leather boots, and does the warranty cover the sole?"
↓ decompose into focused, parallel RAG calls
rag call 1
"return window for leather boots"
rag call 2 ∥
"warranty coverage for wear and tear"
rag call 3 ∥
"is sole damage covered under warranty"
↓ merge chunks · the agent composes one grounded answer
answer built from all three chunk sets, cited, through the guarded lane

This is exactly why we run RAGFlow headless and return chunks instead of answers: the agent stays in control of how many times to ask and how to combine the evidence, rather than the engine collapsing it into one canned reply. One fuzzy question becomes three good ones.

Each call: hybrid = dense + sparse, fused

Real scores for "is wear and tear covered under warranty". Watch the sparse column — that's the exact-keyword signal plain vector cosine throws away:

# docId fused dense sparse snippet
1 gear-care 0.353 0.863 0.134 Proper care is crucial for extending the life of technical gear…
4 warranty 0.339 0.853 0.118 eCommerce provides a Lifetime Warranty on all products to cover…
5 warranty 0.332 0.888 0.094 What it does not cover: the warranty is not a guarantee against…

A reranker (gateway local-rerank → bge cross-encoder) can reorder the top-k further — it lives behind the multimodal profile and is the brittle, plan-deferred piece; hybrid carries the recall win on its own.

RAPTOR: whole-guide summaries

origin RAPTOR is a general, published retrieval technique — a 2024 Stanford paper, "Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval": recursively embed → cluster → summarise chunks into a tree. It's not a RAGFlow invention; RAGFlow ships its own built-in implementation of it.

For "give me an overview of caring for my gear" — a whole-document question — RAPTOR retrieves synthesised summary chunks that don't exist in the source PDF.

retrieved · 14 of 30 chunks are RAPTOR summaries 
"Here is a summary of the provided care and
 warranty notes, keeping careful track of all
 numbers:
  • Exceeding max wash temp voids the materials
    warranty, not workmanship…
  • Aluminum frame + hipbelt: lifetime; fabric
    panels: 60 months…"
Built at ingest from the leaf chunks — the answer covers the whole guide, not one slice.

GraphRAG: multi-hop across docs

origin GraphRAG is Microsoft's method — a Microsoft Research project, open-sourced in 2024: an LLM-built entity/relation knowledge graph with community summaries. It's Microsoft-originated (open source, not proprietary); RAGFlow ships its own implementation of it.

Some answers live between documents. At ingest, GraphRAG extracted an entity/relation graph (52 entities · 5 relations, "light" method) that retrieval can hop across.

knowledge graph · sample relations
ECOMMERCE LIFETIME WARRANTY→PRODUCT
applies to every product made by eCommerce
TRAIL CLUB MEMBERSHIP→POINTS
rewards: earning / redemption ($5 back…)
P.O. BOXES→TENTS & BACKPACKS
shipping restriction · oversized items
"do we run all three, or pick one?" No runtime decision-engine. Hybrid (dense+sparse) is always the substrate. RAPTOR and GraphRAG are ingest-time index-builders, not query-time branches: RAPTOR's summary chunks sit in the same pool as the leaf chunks, so a normal hybrid query just surfaces them when they're the best match (that's how 14 of 30 retrieved chunks came back as summaries). GraphRAG is an extra per-query toggle. So they compose — the results blend together — rather than a classifier choosing one. (A smart query-router that picks a strategy per question is a real thing people build; we don't, yet.)

where it plugs in4The seam — one interface, flag-gated

Everything above sits below one retrieval interface. The app never imports RAGFlow; it calls a single stable retrieve(query, k) method and gets back a list of the app's own chunk objects. Swapping a hand-built stub for RAGFlow changed nothing downstream of that contract. That's the whole point of returning chunks rather than a finished answer: the retrieval engine is a detail behind one interface, and the app owns how the evidence becomes a reply.

our seam The whole RAG service slots in below one retrieval interface — a single retrieve(query, k) method, flag-gated so the engine can be turned on or off — and hands back a list of the app's own chunk type. Behind that interface, a thin read-side client maps RAGFlow's public /api/v1/retrieval response onto that chunk type. Nothing downstream of the contract changed when we swapped the stub for RAGFlow.
